column4: NAD+ precursor acting on the SIRT2/K668 node that controls BubR1 proteasomal turnover (North 2014). Not 5: NR itself was not the compound tested; NMN was
column6: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial in Werner syndrome, a monogenic progeroid disease (Shoji 2025)
column8: Supplement with real paediatric exposure: 8 paediatric-eligible trials on CT.gov, minimum ages down to 1 year, several in ataxia telangiectasia
column10: Oncologic: raising NAD+ availability in a cancer-predisposition syndrome is a theoretical concern, since proliferating tumour cells also depend on NAD+. Renal-neutral in the Werner RCT
column12: Oral, inexpensive, over-the-counter, no monitoring burden

column4: The precursor actually shown to raise BubR1 abundance in vivo (North 2014, Fig 6D-E)
column6: In vivo rodent evidence only, and in WILD-TYPE mice, not a BubR1 model. Never administered to a BubR1-deficient animal
column8: Supplement; only 1 paediatric-eligible trial found - materially thinner than NR
column10: Same theoretical oncologic concern as NR
column12: Oral, OTC since FDA restored supplement status Sept 2025

column4: Anti-CD38; CD38 is the principal NAD+-consuming ectoenzyme, so blockade raises NAD+ at the same proximal node. The only approved drug the search found acting on the abundance tier
column6: NAD+-raising via CD38 blockade is preclinical; no human trial tests it for this purpose
column8: Approved drug; US label states paediatric safety and effectiveness NOT established, but 7 paediatric-eligible trials exist
column10: Profound immunosuppression and infection risk; loss of immune surveillance in a cancer-predisposed child; infusion reactions; interference with blood typing
column12: IV infusion, specialist administration, high cost

column4: Clears senescent cells - the first downstream consequence of CIN, not the defect itself
column6: Two open-label human trials with mechanism biomarkers (Justice 2019 IPF; Hickson 2019 DKD as corrected by its 2020 corrigendum)
column8: Dasatinib is FDA-approved with a paediatric indication from age 1 (Ph+ CML chronic phase; newly diagnosed Ph+ ALL with chemotherapy), with long-term paediatric CML follow-up
column10: Growth impairment is documented for TKIs in children and this child is already growth-restricted (HP:0004322); CYP3A4 interaction with future chemotherapy; genomic-instability disorders show exquisite chemo/radiation sensitivity (Nakano 2024). NOTE none of the 22 D+Q trials enrolled anyone under 18
column12: Oral, intermittent hit-and-run dosing; prescription oncology agent requiring monitoring

column4: Flavonoid senolytic; same downstream node as D+Q
column6: Rodent in vivo senolytic data; human trials under way without published biomarker outcomes
column10: Minimal toxicity data at senolytic doses; theoretical oncologic concern

column6: Rodent senolytic in vivo; human data is oncologic, not senolytic
column8: Investigational; paediatric oncology trials exist but no approval
column10: Dose-limiting thrombocytopenia; no paediatric approval; oncologic setting only

column6: In vivo rodent (aged wild-type mice, Xu 2015); not a BubR1 model
column8: Approved with a paediatric indication for steroid-refractory acute GVHD from age 12 (Jakafi label); narrow and acute, so long-term paediatric data are limited
column10: Immunosuppression is the mechanism, not a side effect; infection and reactivation risk; cytopenias; suppressing innate immune surveillance in a cancer-predisposed child (cf. Bakhoum 2018)

column4: Same JAK1/2 SASP mechanism as ruxolitinib
column6: Class inference only; Xu 2015 did not establish this agent specifically
column8: Approved adult drug; US Olumiant label states paediatric safety and effectiveness NOT established, but 16 paediatric-eligible trials exist. See the rubric-fit note in the report

column4: mTOR inhibition modulates SASP translation, but the agent is pleiotropic and this is one effect among many
column6: Rodent geroprotection well established; not a BubR1 model
column8: Approved from age 13 for renal transplant prophylaxis; extensive paediatric off-label use in vascular anomalies and TSC with published safety data. Label states efficacy NOT established below 13
column10: Immunosuppression; impaired wound healing; metabolic and growth effects; proteinuria is a concern against congenital nephrocalcinosis
column12: Oral but requires therapeutic drug-level monitoring

column4: Geroprotective/senomorphic via NF-kB and SASP damping; distal and pleiotropic, not directed at the defect
column6: Rodent in vivo plus large human observational data; weak for the SASP mechanism specifically
column8: Immediate-release metformin is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in paediatric patients 10-16 years, with decades of paediatric safety data. Extended-release is NOT paediatrically established
column10: Renal: metformin requires adequate renal function, relevant given nephrocalcinosis present since birth; GI intolerance
column12: Oral, extremely inexpensive, widely available, familiar to any paediatrician

column4: HSP90 inhibitor. Suijkerbuijk 2010 showed mutant BubR1 is an HSP90 client: geldanamycin severely reduced mutant but not wild-type BubR1, and CHX+GA removed virtually all of it. Predicted to destroy the residual protein this child depends on
column6: Also gate G2: this is Tang 2011's aneuploidy-selective agent, i.e. selective cytotoxicity toward the cells that constitute this patient

column4: NAMPT inhibitor. Lowers NAD+, the exact opposite of the intended direction, and would be predicted to lower BubR1

PARP inhibitor. Spares NAD+ in principle, so it reaches the abundance node - but PARP inhibitors are associated with secondary MDS/AML, and giving a genotoxic agent to a child with a constitutional chromosomal-instability and cancer-predisposition syndrome inverts the risk calculus. Gated on the harm limb rather than the mechanism limb
